faq.a: It penetrates CSF slowly and does not achieve fungicidal levels; amphotericin B plus flucytosine is required for rapid clearance.
faq.q: Why is fluconazole not sufficient for cryptococcal meningitis in severe disease?

faq.a: No; KOH is useful for superficial lesions only. Systemic disease needs culture or antigen testing.
faq.q: Can a negative KOH rule out a deep fungal infection?

faq.a: Candida albicans overgrowth, often after antibiotics, steroids or in HIV.
faq.q: What is the most common cause of oral thrush in adults?

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV patient presents with headache and photophobia – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Perform serum CrAg LFA; a positive result predicts meningitis and guides urgent lumbar puncture.

A neutropenic patient on chemotherapy develops fever and pleuritic chest pain; chest X‑ray shows a halo sign – which organism is most likely and what empirical therapy should you start? — Invasive Aspergillus; start voriconazole if available, otherwise amphotericin B.

A diabetic with a painful, erythematous foot ulcer shows branching septate hyphae on KOH – what is the likely pathogen and initial management? — Likely dermatophyte or Fusarium; start oral terbinafine and debride wound.

A child with persistent oral white plaques after antibiotics – what distinguishes Candida thrush from oral leukoplakia? — Candida is removable with a swab and responds to antifungals; leukoplakia is non‑removable and requires biopsy.
Why should central venous catheters be removed in candidemia? — Catheters act as a nidus; removal improves clearance and reduces mortality.
What are the contraindications to using amphotericin B in a patient with renal failure? — High nephrotoxicity; consider liposomal formulation or switch to fluconazole if organism susceptible.
How does HIV increase risk for cryptococcal disease? — CD4 <100 cells/µL impairs cell‑mediated immunity, allowing encapsulated yeast to proliferate in CNS.

A patient on long‑term steroids develops a scaly, annular rash on the trunk – which test confirms dermatophyte infection and what is the treatment of choice? — KOH prep showing hyphae; treat with oral terbinafine for >2 weeks.
ai.title: Fungal Infections Overview
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A concise clinical guide to common fungal infections seen in low‑resource African hospitals, focusing on presentation, diagnosis without advanced labs, and pragmatic management.

b: Superficial – skin, hair, nails
Mucosal – oral, genital, esophageal
Systemic – bloodstream, CNS, lungs
sections.p: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that can cause superficial, mucosal or systemic disease, especially in immunocompromised patients. In East Africa, Candida, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma and dermatophytes are most frequent.

b: Yeasts: budding, round cells (Candida, Cryptococcus)
Moulds: septate hyphae, conidia (Aspergillus, dermatophytes)
Capsule: thick polysaccharide capsule in Cryptococcus
sections.p: Fungi have cell walls of chitin and β‑glucan, reproduce by spores (sexual or asexual) and grow as yeasts (single cells) or moulds (filamentous hyphae).

b: Inhalation of spores – Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Aspergillus
Skin contact with contaminated soil or animal droppings – dermatophytes, Sporothrix
Endogenous overgrowth – Candida from gut or vaginal flora
sections.p: Most infections are acquired from the environment or endogenous flora; few are transmitted person‑to‑person.

b: Candida albicans – oropharyngeal thrush, vaginitis, invasive candidemia
Cryptococcus neoformans – meningitis in HIV
Histoplasma capsulatum – disseminated disease in HIV or chronic lung disease
Dermatophytes – tinea corporis, capitis, pedis
sections.p: Clinical syndromes vary by host immunity and portal of entry.

b: KOH wet mount – hyphae or yeast buds in skin scrapings
India ink stain of CSF – encapsulated yeast (Cryptococcus)
Gram stain / Giemsa – budding yeasts in blood
Rapid antigen lateral flow – cryptococcal antigen in serum/CSF
sections.p: In low‑resource settings rely on bedside clues, simple microscopy and point‑of‑care tests.

t.b: Does the specimen contain fungal elements? – Positive shows hyphae or yeast; negative does not rule out deep infection.
Is there encapsulated yeast? – Positive confirms cryptococcal meningitis; if unavailable, send CSF for culture and treat empirically in high‑risk HIV.
Is cryptococcal antigen present? – Positive predicts meningitis; if test not available, start fluconazole empirically in advanced HIV.
Is there candidemia? – Positive guides therapy; if culture unavailable, treat septic patient with risk factors (central line, broad antibiotics) with echinocandin if possible.

b: Candida – fluconazole for mucosal disease; echinocandin or amphotericin B for invasive disease; remove catheters.
Cryptococcus – high‑dose fluconazole or amphotericin B + flucytosine for meningitis; maintain ART in HIV.
Histoplasma – itraconazole for mild‑moderate; amphotericin B for severe disseminated disease.
Dermatophytes – topical azoles or terbinafine; keep skin dry, treat contacts.
sections.p: Therapy combines antifungal agents with correction of predisposing factors.

b: Identify risk groups (HIV, neutropenia, indwelling lines).
Know bedside tests that replace culture (KOH, India ink, CrAg LFA).
Remember first‑line drug class and why alternatives are avoided (e.g., fluconazole avoided in severe cryptococcal meningitis because of poor CSF penetration).
Recognize red‑flag signs needing urgent care: meningitis, septic shock, massive candidemia.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever with altered mental status in HIV – suspect cryptococcal meningitis
Rapidly progressive skin necrosis in neutropenic patient – possible invasive mould infection
Persistent high‑grade fever despite antibiotics and central line – consider candidemia
